facts.claim: "Family (Blackbird)" is a one-track single by Badflower, 4:08 long, on Big Machine Records / John Varvatos Records, with a 2022-07-01 release date on Deezer.
The composer credits for "Family (Blackbird)" are the four band members: Josh Katz, Joey Morrow, Alex Espiritu and Anthony Sonetti.

The track is an orchestral version of the band's song "Family". Amazon Music lists it as "Family (Blackbird / Amazon Original)" and dates it April 1, 2022. Josh Katz later said the band recorded two orchestral songs and released only "Family".
The orchestral version was first available only on Amazon Music, and was later released on all platforms.

The original "Family" was the lead single from Badflower's second album, This Is How the World Ends (released September 24, 2021). Lyrically it reflects Katz's strained relationship with his own family.

Katz said the song is very important to him. He wrote about spending years trying to understand why he distances himself from the people he cares about most, and why dealing with his family as an adult feels uncomfortable.
Katz said that at age 30 he realized his own role in the "bad energy" in his relationships. He sent the song to his family and began having the conversations the song says he can't have.
Katz compared the "brutal honesty" of "Family" to the band's breakout single "Ghost", though "Family" comes from a different perspective.
In 2022 Katz said "Family" is a really hard song to sing live, though it has gotten easier.

Badflower is a Los Angeles band. The re-formed lineup is Josh Katz (vocals/guitar), Joey Morrow (guitar), Anthony Sonetti (drums) and Alex Espiritu (bass). Their debut album OK, I'm Sick came out in early 2019 on Big Machine, and "Ghost" was their first modern rock radio hit in 2018.

research.lineage: Badflower sit in the Los Angeles hard rock and post-grunge tradition, with a Sunset Strip-inspired swagger and comparisons to Royal Blood and early Silverchair.

draft:
The math in **Family (Blackbird)** is brutal and simple: "First 15 years I'm the favourite son," Josh Katz sings, and then the second half of a thirty-year life arrives as its mirror image, the hated one. There's no event in between, no single fight that explains the turn. That's the most honest thing about the song. Estrangement rarely has a date. It accumulates, one missed call and one unsent birthday card at a time, until a person looks up and can't find the way back.

Katz has said he spent years trying to understand why he pushes away the people he cares about most, and why being with his family as an adult feels so uncomfortable. The lyrics don't solve that. They circle it. The narrator is drunk and missing home, dreaming of a version where "everyone still likes me," and the confession comes in a flat, damning list: he made his sisters cry, he calls himself a shitty brother, nobody's friend. Then comes the line that holds the whole ache: "I never say 'I love you' even though I want to." Wanting and doing have come apart, and he can feel the gap without being able to close it.

What keeps the song from becoming pure self-flagellation is that it won't stay in one emotional key. Guilt keeps sliding into grievance. "This is all my fault" sits a few lines from "Is everyone against me?" The last verse goes further, scoffing that families only say "I love you" because they're supposed to, then insisting, "And most families lie, but I meant it every time." That contradicts what he said earlier, and the song lets it stand. Self-hatred and self-defense live in the same body here. Anyone who has been the difficult one at the holiday table will recognize both.

This is the orchestral reworking of the lead single from *This Is How the World Ends*, and it pulls Badflower well away from their Los Angeles hard-rock swagger. A clean electric guitar picks out arpeggiated chords over bass and a steady, unhurried drum kit. The production is polished and open, with room around each instrument. Katz's voice is a little raspy, held long and mournful in the middle of his range, and a quiet harmony slips in behind him on certain words, as if someone else were briefly carrying the weight. The repeated cry of "What happened to this family?" lands harder at this pace. There's nowhere for it to hide.

Katz has said the song is hard to sing live. He also said that after writing it, he sent it to his family and started having the conversations the narrator can't have. That makes the song a kind of bridge he built before he could cross it.

It sticks because it says the thing you've been too proud or too scared to say to your own people, and it lets you hear how much it costs to say it.
